---
title: "Quiz: Hough transform for lines"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Lines are written in normal form $x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = \rho$, $\theta \in [0°, 180°)$, origin at the image centre, $y$ up.

---

**Q1.** What does a single edge point become in the $(\theta, \rho)$ parameter space, and what does that curve represent?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which lines pass through the point?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A sinusoid $\rho(\theta) = x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta$. Each point of the curve is one line through the edge point: the curve is the set of all lines that pass through it.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why is the slope–intercept form $y = mx + c$ a poor choice of parameters for a Hough accumulator?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What are $m$ and $c$ of a vertical line?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The slope is unbounded: a vertical line has $m = \infty$, and nearly vertical lines have very large $m$ and $c$. A finite grid of bins over $(m, c)$ cannot contain all lines. The normal form has $\theta \in [0°, 180°)$ and $|\rho|$ at most half the image diagonal, so a finite grid covers every line.
:::

---

**Q3.** A line is drawn as a dashed line: only every other group of 10 pixels is present. Compared with the solid line, what happens to its peak in the accumulator?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each point votes independently.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The peak stays at the same $(\theta, \rho)$ and has about half the height (half as many edge points vote for it). The gaps themselves do not matter; only the number of points on the line does. If half the height is still above the threshold, the line is found.
:::

---

**Q4.** Without non-maximum suppression, a single straight edge gives several detections. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Do all votes of one line land in exactly one bin?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Edge positions are rounded to pixels and slightly noisy, and the grid is discrete, so the votes of one line spread over a few neighbouring $(\theta, \rho)$ bins. Several of them exceed the threshold, and each becomes a nearly identical line. NMS keeps only the bin that is the maximum in its neighbourhood.
:::

---

**Q5.** You make the bins ten times finer to measure the angle of a line more precisely, and the line is no longer detected. What happened?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many votes does each small bin get?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The edge points of a real line are not exactly collinear. With very small bins their votes spread over many bins, so no single bin reaches the threshold: the peak dissolves. Bins should be about as large as the scatter of the votes (about 1 px in $\rho$ and a fraction of a degree to a degree in $\theta$). For more precision, refine the peak afterwards, for example by fitting a line to the points that voted for it.
:::

---

**Q6.** An edge point has gradient direction 30°. With gradient voting, for which lines does it vote? Why does this reduce false detections in clutter?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How is the gradient related to the direction of the edge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The gradient is perpendicular to the edge, so it is the normal of the line the point lies on: the point votes only for $\theta \approx 30°$ (within a small window), at its own $\rho$. A random clutter point now casts a few votes instead of one per angle, and for a bin to collect many votes the points must be collinear **and** have gradients perpendicular to that line. Chance alignments of clutter rarely satisfy both.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Show that the curves of two different points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ cross at the $\theta$ whose normal is perpendicular to $(x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1)$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Subtract the two equations $\rho = x_i\cos\theta + y_i\sin\theta$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At a crossing both give the same $\rho$: $(x_1 - x_2)\cos\theta + (y_1 - y_2)\sin\theta = 0$, i.e. $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \cdot (\mathbf p_1 - \mathbf p_2) = 0$. The normal is perpendicular to the difference of the points, so the line with this normal and $\rho = x_1\cos\theta + y_1\sin\theta$ contains both points. In $[0°, 180°)$ there is exactly one such $\theta$.
:::

---

**Q8.** How are the Hough transform for lines and the Radon transform related?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What is the integral of a binary edge image along a line?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The [Radon transform](../radon/lec.qmd) integrates an image along every line $(\theta, \rho)$. For a binary edge image this integral counts the edge pixels on the line, which is the number of votes in the Hough bin $(\theta, \rho)$. The Hough accumulator is a discretised Radon transform of the edge map; the Hough transform looks for its peaks, while the Radon day uses it for reconstruction.
:::
